questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Repeated Integral Defined Over a Type I Region
questions.worked_solution:
The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{1/x}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{x}^{1/x}y\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{x}^{1/x}dx \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-{x}^{2})dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}(\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}-1)\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}(\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}-1)\,dx & =\frac{1}{2}{[-\frac{1}{3{x}^{3}}-x]}_{1/2}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\frac{1}{3}+1-(\frac{8}{3}+\frac{1}{2})] \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{11}{6}) \\  & =\frac{11}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Double Integral Defined Over a Type I Region
questions.problem:
Evaluate the double integral
${∬}_{D}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dA,$
where $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the line
$y=1-x$ and the coordinate axes.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14067291/assets/95ebd0a4eb874972b459e53eecf1d57650f63284698fcad967c09620ac01cd99.png)

Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- The line $y=1-x$ intercepts the $x$-axis at $x=1.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$0\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14067291/assets/d048f20f2299722cee598cc1005237627ecdd7643e996b269f26b5a096f01f2f.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1-x}
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dA={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dy\,dx
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{-x+1}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dy]\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-\frac{1}{1+x+y}]}_{0}^{-x+1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{1}{1+x+(1-x)}-(-\frac{1}{1+x+0}))\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{1+x})dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{1+x})dx & ={[-\frac{1}{2}x+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x)]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-(0+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral When the Limits are Not Given
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14067291/assets/ce364dc7c6c4fc5e229fdeb0809b3779bf1052c60d956deb742731f34e54562d.png)

If $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the lines $y=2x,$ $x=0,$ and $y=4,$ as shown above, then ${∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\sqrt{x}\,dA=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. 

- To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =4 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x$-limits are 
$0\le x\le 2.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14067291/assets/54f366679684823341bab818459ce5fc884ebbdd2376e800b781d1b832c4ba64.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,2x\le y\le 4}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{2x}^{4}{y}^{2}\sqrt{x}\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Double Integral Defined Over a Type I Region
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14067291/assets/6accbfcccdf910acca3aab9f1a12d0ab35c4da683fe78d6ca2d7ada88f28767c.png)

Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\,dA,$
where $D$ is the finite region above the $x$-axis enclosed by the curve $y=1-{x}^{2}$ and the line $x=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- We already know the intersection of the curve with the line $y=0.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$0\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14067291/assets/db0dd47348fb2f9a97c9e0514f74adae05830de7e03f1aea2886eaa95701200e.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1-{x}^{2}}
$$

So, we can express the integral, as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\,dA={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}{x}^{2}\,dy\,dx
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}{x}^{2}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}[y]_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(1-{x}^{2}-0)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}-{x}^{4})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}-{x}^{4})\,dx & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{5}-0 \\  & =\frac{2}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Repeated Integral Defined Over a Type I Region
questions.worked_solution:
The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡x[{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡x[\,y\,]_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,dx & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-2) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$
